title: Comment on: What is going on with ceiling fans
body:
I just wish there was some way to replace the LEDs on these things when they inevitably die. And, no matter what large number of years or decades are slathered on the box, inevitably at least one LED panel will blow out three to six months after purchase, nominally still in warranty but good luck getting any service under it, I'm sure. If there was, there could be a place for at least some of these in a house, but the amount of crap that you have no choice but to throw out as soon as the LEDs fry is insane.
This is why my "fancy" lighting fixture is an old track (whose proprietary lights died a long time ago) wrapped with an extension cable with 5 standard sockets on it, and some standard light bulbs in it. We dress it up with ribbons and stuff for the seasons. It doesn't look as nice as any of the things in that article, not even the gaudy and tasteless ones, but when a bulb burn out, I put a new one in and get on with life, I don't throw out an entire fan and buy a new one.
I'm old enough to remember when I was promised LEDs would last approximately forever without having to be replaced.

title: Comment on: ADHD, autism or complex trauma? [pdf]
body:
Consider two approaches: one is to spend hours ruminating on your experiences every day to form insights and approaches to tackle new problems and make new progress. The other is to panic at the slightest sign of anything, compartmentalize everything and get stuck in fruitless thought loops constantly, making very little progress to integrate information or have insights. Say both of those take the same immense amounts of energy, but maybe the former would have a better shot at fighting active abuse, you know? In my experience, calculated thought is far superior to fruitless panic. In this way one could be considered "stronger" than the other even though both are technically undesirable (because constant rumination over everything is actually terrible, for example).
Real example based on real self-doubt across multiple friends I know.

title: Comment on: Every SaaS business will become a harness around a model
body:
This is the AI companies' fantasy, to replace simple, efficient, deterministic computing with expensive LLM calls. It'll be bad for customers, bad for users, bad for the environment, bad for everybody except the companies selling it.
I'm a heavy AI user and haven't written code by hand in a long time (and probably won't until Advent of Code, honestly) but I'm already sick of people using AI to replace code at things that code excels at and AI is no better at, just slower and more expensive.
It isn't just driven by the AI companies, either. I've already seen it internally, with developers who need diagnostic tools creating Claude skills, and in the excitement of adopting AI, barely noticing that they're incredibly slow, expensive, unreliable, and even slow to create compared to the script or diagnostic endpoint they would created in the past. And they're surprised to learn that Claude skills suffer from bitrot and cross-repo dependencies just like traditional software: somebody's Claude skill fails because it wasn't updated to match changes elsewhere, and it takes much longer to realize that a conversation with Claude is going wrong than if a script or an endpoint returns an error.
When code is the best solution, by all means use AI to write it! But don't use AI instead when AI isn't fit for purpose.

title: Comment on: Former SR-71 engineer talks NASA's Blackbird revival program
body:
Fair correction on the altitude (still in the lower bounds of the balloons, as I mentioned).
The SR-71 already flew in the configuration I mentioned. It's the YF-12C (a converted SR-71).
Recovering and converting another sure is more expensive than one missile, but it's a reusable platform.
A ground missile able to reach those balloons is more expensive than a modernized SR-71 sortie. High-altitude, precision missiles are also not allocated for this task. China can launch dozens of balloons for cheap, and spending one multi-million-dollar missile on each is insanity. Even the long range air-to-air ones are too expensive for that.
The SR-71 (as a new YF-12D interceptor) makes more sense. It can take multiple balloons in one flight with cheap shorter range air-to-air missiles (or maybe even cheaper weapons, for a balloon a laser would do), then go home and do that over and over again.

title: Comment on: Scientists invent underwater umbrellas to protect coral reefs
body:
Looks like a feel good solution mostly. Good for donations, but is not so clear how much would solve the problem. The solution to environmental problems is never cheap so the best use of resources is to use money where it can assure that the problem will never happen. After if happens common people can't fix it. Is too expensive.
A problem is that corals need algae to photosinthesize so too much shadow is also bad.
Another is that the shadowed water will be still hot, because the cold water moves away with the tides and oceanic temperature inertia is too powerful. So now corals could have two problems instead one problem. Feel good solution.
A better focus would be to use some kind of system to move deep water up using the reef topology. Would be noisy and obtain permits will be a real pain in the ass, but at least could work for a while to protect entire ecosystems in small areas that can be used later to seed other areas around.
In the meanwhile as this is not easy, this small umbrellas are time consuming to build and can dislodge and hit other corals potentially breaking or damaging fragile species that need decades to grow, a floating and well anchored second hand jumping bed would be much more efficient, relatively less risky to crash against submerged corals, and a little more durable. Many owners of jumping beds with holes on it, would be glad to get rid of... donate them for free for a good cause. At least this is needed just in summer and will need to be removed before winter storms turns it into garbage. Small fishes will use also this platforms for refuge so corals could also benefit of that.
Watching the health of the colony constantly to see if there is too much shadow is essential, Also place it out of the fishermen way and never on ship routes. And this can't be used in areas with seals.

title: Comment on: City building games have a Soul Problem pt.2
body:
It's quite possible to do all that. Most AAA titles do by now. But creating all that detailed content at multiple levels of detail is a big job. GTA VI cost between $1.5 billion and $2 billion to produce. When you do those big zooms, vast amounts of data has to be shuttled in and out of the GPU. VRAM is too expensive to keep it all live.
There are some other current problems. GPU prices have not come down. 
If you want a big, high-detailed world, you need a few hundred dollars of GPU.
GPUs on laptops tend to be underpowered, and if you make the GPU work to its full capacity, it runs down the battery.
One of my interests is technology for large metaverses with high detail and good performance. Everybody who made metaverse noise during the boom failed at that. Second Life, which is a large metaverse with good detail but slow performance, is about as good as it gets. 
(It's been improving recently; they've hired some good graphics developers.)
Improbable's Morpheus/M-Squared [1] looked promising, but the site hasn't been updated in a year and the Discord community seems to have died. They usually run with "cloud rendering" (each user ties up a dedicated gamer PC in a data center), which is too expensive except for special events. Roblox is probably the only other serious US player working on this. Unreal Engine 5 can do big, static worlds that have lots of instancing, but that's achieved using large amounts of preprocessing, optimization, and performance debugging.
The underlying problem is that good simulated cities are about as interesting as real cities. Kind of boring. Second Life has a terrible problem with new users. At the start, you're in a big world the size of Los Angeles with about 40,000 people spread around. You don't know anybody. You have no idea what to do first. There is no obvious goal. There is no built in game. The system itself is completely indifferent to you, like real cities. You can explore the huge user-built world freely, but only when some…

title: Comment on: One month coding with GLM 5.3 Flash
body:
> why bother trying to make training and inference efficient when you can just throw hardware/money at the problem.
Sure, for certain bleeding edge research path-finding, any optimization is premature but that's tiny compared to deployed end-user product scale. The biggest constraints frontier cloud model providers face are: 1. Getting enough of the hardware they want, 2. Capital, 3. Talent (and #3 is a largely a function of #2 & #1).
Given the raw economics, it would be foolish to not have efficiency teams fast-following their deployments as closely as possible. We're seeing direct and indirect evidence of significant efficiency improvements across all the frontier providers and the rate seems to be increasing. The coming OAI & ANT IPOs hinge on demonstrating they can serve many use cases beyond software dev profitably at what they are willing to pay, which is generally less than software dev. The trend is clearly "the higher volume the use case, the less they're willing to pay".
